title: Regal Wealth x Redwood — technical deep dive: audit logs + KMS/HSM
summary: Technical deep dive focused on Redwood audit logging (fields, event types, and export options) and encryption key management for regulated environments. Regal Wealth asked for: (1) a clear audit log schema that maps to SOC/SIEM workflows (Splunk), (2) details on log export and retention controls for Private/VPC deployments, and (3) customer-managed keys and HSM alignment (AWS KMS today; potential on-prem HSM later). Redwood clarified current capabilities and what is configuration vs roadmap, and agreed to share a sample audit payload + evidence pack index under NDA.
topics: Audit log event types and fields (auth, admin, inference request, config changes)
Correlation IDs / request IDs for tracing
Export patterns: S3/object storage, SIEM (Splunk), webhook/streaming vs batch
Retention controls and data minimization (prompts, outputs, metadata)
Customer-managed keys (AWS KMS) and envelope encryption
HSM considerations for on-prem / Private deployments
Operational workflows: access reviews, break-glass, incident response
action_items: Fatima Noor (Redwood) — Send Regal a sample audit log payload (sanitized) + field dictionary; include notes on which fields are optional/configurable — due 2025-06-05
Naomi Feldman (Redwood) — Share evidence pack index + SOC 2 report access process (NDA gate) and point to encryption diagram — due 2025-06-05
Chris Donnelly (Regal) — Confirm required export target (Splunk HEC vs S3 + Splunk add-on) and preferred format (JSON Lines vs CSV) — due 2025-06-06
Avery Johnson (Redwood) — Schedule follow-up to review Regal’s security questionnaire section on logging/encryption and align on Private deployment topology — due 2025-06-07
next_steps: Redwood to provide audit log sample and mapping guidance for Splunk ingestion.
Regal to confirm whether logs must exclude prompt/output content entirely (metadata-only) for their policy.
Redwood to outline KMS customer-managed key option for Private/VPC and key rotation expectations.
Book a 30-min follow-up with Regal Security + Platform to validate controls and unblock procurement checklist.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Regal Wealth x Redwood — technical deep dive: audit logs + KMS/HSM
Date: 2025-06-03
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min

Attendees:
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Fatima Noor (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference, Security/Compliance)
- Maya Patel (Regal Wealth, Director InfoSec)
- Chris Donnelly (Regal Wealth, Platform Eng Lead)
- Jonas Weber (Regal Wealth, GRC/Risk)


[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. Today is supposed to be the deeper dive on audit logs and KMS stuff, which came up in your checklist. Fatima’s here to go through how it works technically, and Naomi for anything compliance-y.

[00:15] Maya Patel: Yep, thanks Avery. We’re trying to close gaps on logging and encryption. Basically our SOC team will ask “show me the audit trail” and we need to see it end-to-end.

[00:26] Chris Donnelly: And I’m looking for practical integration. Like where do logs go, can I ship them into Splunk, do we get correlation IDs, that kind of thing.

[00:36] Fatima Noor: Perfect. I can start with what an “audit event” is in Redwood terms, then talk export patterns. Also I’ll caveat up front — hosted API versus Dedicated versus Private have slightly different surfaces, but the audit schema is consistent.

[00:52] Jonas Weber: Great. And just to set context, we’re a wealth manager. We’re under SEC/FINRA oversight. We’re not doing medical, but we treat customer data as confidential. We need retention controls and we need to be able to prove who did what.

[01:09] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[01:11] Fatima Noor: Cool. So audit logs: we generate events for (1) auth and access, (2) administrative/config changes, and (3) inference activity. The “inference activity” piece is where people get nervous because they think it’s logging prompts and outputs.

[01:27] Maya Patel: Yeah, that’s exactly it. We generally want metadata, not content.

[01:31] Fatima Noor: Right. By default for regulated deployments we recommend metadata-only audit events, and then separately you can have application-level logging if you want to capture prompts/outcomes in your own system under your own controls.

[01:45] Naomi Feldman: And from compliance standpoint, we’re careful not to over-collect. The product’s designed so you can keep the audit trail without storing sensitive request bodies in Redwood logs.

[01:56] Chris Donnelly: Ok. So what’s in an event. Like fields.

[02:01] Fatima Noor: Let me list the common fields. There’s an event_id (UUID), event_time (RFC3339 timestamp), event_type, and then actor fields: actor_type (user/service), actor_id, and if it’s SSO we’ll show the external subject / SAML NameID mapping.

[02:20] Chris Donnelly: Wait, you said SAML. That’s only on Private or also Dedicated?

[02:24] Naomi Feldman: Dedicated and Private both support SSO/SAML for the Console. Hosted orgs also can, depending on plan, but for your case we’ve been scoping Private in a VPC so yes.

[02:35] Fatima Noor: Continuing. Resource fields: resource_type (project, model, deployment, api_key), resource_id, and an action like create/update/delete/rotate_key, etc.

[02:48] Fatima Noor: For inference events specifically: request_id (we call it request_id but you can treat it like a correlation id), model, model_version, region, deployment_mode (dedicated/private), and then performance/cost metadata: prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens, latency_ms, queue_time_ms.

[03:09] Maya Patel: Does it include IP address?

[03:11] Fatima Noor: Yes, there is client_ip for API calls, plus user_agent if applicable. On Private you can also capture source VPC endpoint id if you’re routing through PrivateLink-type patterns, depending on cloud.

[03:25] Chris Donnelly: And what about “success/failure.”

[03:28] Fatima Noor: status_code, error_class, and an error_message that is intentionally short / sanitized. We don’t dump stack traces into audit logs.

[03:38] Jonas Weber: For admins, we need “who changed retention settings” or “who changed routing policy.” That exists?

[03:44] Fatima Noor: Yes. Config changes are admin events: policy_change, retention_update, log_export_update, key_rotation_config_update, things like that. They include before/after hashes. Not the full config blob unless you choose that. (And we generally don’t recommend storing full config deltas if they can contain sensitive endpoints.)

[04:08] Maya Patel: Before/after hashes are fine. We just need to show it changed and who did it.

[04:13] Chris Donnelly: Ok. Export patterns. This is the big thing. We need to get it into Splunk.

[04:18] Fatima Noor: Yep. There are basically three patterns we see:
1) Batch export to object storage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob) in JSON Lines.
2) Streaming export to a SIEM endpoint (often Splunk HEC) via HTTPS.
3) Forward to a log agent inside your environment (like Fluent Bit) if you’re running Private on Kubernetes.

[04:40] Chris Donnelly: Which ones are actually available today.

[04:43] Fatima Noor: For Private-in-VPC: S3 export is GA. Streaming webhook export is available but we usually gate it behind a short validation because we don’t want it to become a backpressure issue. For on-prem Kubernetes, forwarding to your log agent is typical — we write JSON to a file/STDOUT and you pick it up.

[05:07] Chris Donnelly: Our standard is Splunk. We can do HEC or we can do S3 + Splunk add-on. HEC tends to get blocked by networking, but S3 is easy.

[05:17] Maya Patel: If it’s S3, we also need to ensure bucket encryption and that we can use our own keys.

[05:23] Fatima Noor: Yep, for S3 export in AWS you can configure SSE-KMS and point it to your CMK. That’s part of the export config.

[05:32] Naomi Feldman: And we can document the shared responsibility. In a Private deployment inside your AWS account, you own the bucket and the KMS key. Redwood writes to it with an IAM role you control.

[05:44] Jonas Weber: That sounds good. But I want clarity: are logs stored anywhere else first? Like in your system for a day then shipped?

[05:53] Fatima Noor: Good question. In Private, logs are written to the audit log store inside the deployment boundary, and then exported on schedule. There is a short buffering window for delivery (minutes), but retention is governed by your config. If you set retention to, say, 7 days local, it will be purged after 7 days.

[06:15] Maya Patel: Can we set it to zero local?

[06:17] Fatima Noor: We can set it very low. Practically, you need some buffering for reliability, especially if the export target is temporarily unavailable. But you can set, for example, 24 hours or 6 hours depending on the deployment. We should confirm what your policy allows.

[06:35] Chris Donnelly: We usually want 30-90 days in Splunk, and minimal local retention.

[06:40] Jonas Weber: Also immutability. Like WORM storage.

[06:44] Fatima Noor: Redwood itself doesn’t provide WORM, but if you export to S3 you can use Object Lock / retention policies on the bucket. That’s the normal pattern.

[06:55] Maya Patel: Ok, that’s acceptable.

[06:58] Avery Johnson: And we can include that in the architecture doc — “use S3 Object Lock” as recommended.

[07:04] Chris Donnelly: On the fields: do you log API keys? Like actual secrets?

[07:09] Fatima Noor: No. We log key_id, not the secret. For auth events we log “api_key_used=true” and the key identifier. Same with tokens.

[07:18] Maya Patel: For identity, we need RBAC events too.

[07:22] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we have events for role assignment changes and group mapping changes (SAML groups, SCIM provisioning if enabled). That’s in the admin event set.

[07:34] Chris Donnelly: SCIM is a question too. But we can do that later.

[07:37] Fatima Noor: Yep.

[07:39] Jonas Weber: Can you show a sample event? Even if it’s fake.

[07:43] Fatima Noor: I can read out an example verbally, and then I’ll send a sanitized JSON after the call. Example inference event:
- event_type: "inference.request"
- event_time: "2025-06-03T16:12:44Z"
- actor_type: "service"
- actor_id: "svc-7f2..."
- request_id: "req_9c1..."
- model: "llama-3.1-70b"
- model_version: "2025-05-18"
- region: "us-east-1"
- prompt_tokens: 812
- completion_tokens: 146
- latency_ms: 1180
- status_code: 200
- policy: "regal-prod"

[08:25] Chris Donnelly: Do you include the endpoint route, like /v1/chat/completions.

[08:29] Fatima Noor: Yes, route and api_version.

[08:33] Maya Patel: What about “prompt hash.” Some vendors do a hash so you can later prove something without storing it.

[08:40] Fatima Noor: We can include a request_body_hash option. It’s off by default. We’ve seen regulated customers use it when they need non-repudiation without storing payloads. But it has tradeoffs — you need to be careful about canonicalization.

[08:58] Jonas Weber: That’s interesting. Not sure we need it.

[09:02] Maya Patel: We probably don’t. We prefer to log in the app if needed.

[09:06] Chris Donnelly: Export format. JSON lines is fine. But we need stable schema and versioning.

[09:13] Fatima Noor: Yes, schema_version is in every record. When we add fields, we do it additively. We don’t remove fields without deprecation.

[09:22] Chris Donnelly: Great.

[09:24] Avery Johnson: You also asked about KMS/HSM. Want to transition to that?

[09:28] Maya Patel: Yes. Specifically: “customer-managed keys” is a checkbox for us, and we need to understand whether you support HSM-backed keys.

[09:37] Naomi Feldman: I can start. At a high level: data is encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest. For Private deployments, you can use your cloud-native KMS for at-rest encryption of storage volumes, object storage exports, and secrets. Whether the underlying KMS uses HSM is generally a property of AWS KMS / CloudHSM.

[09:57] Maya Patel: So do we bring a key, or do you create it.

[10:00] Naomi Feldman: Typically you create and own the key in your account, and we’re granted permission to use it for encryption operations needed by the deployment. We don’t take possession of key material.

[10:13] Chris Donnelly: Is it envelope encryption.

[10:15] Fatima Noor: Yes, envelope. We have a data key per encrypted blob/object, then the data key is encrypted by your CMK. For storage volumes it’s your EBS encryption config, etc.

[10:28] Maya Patel: Key rotation.

[10:31] Fatima Noor: For KMS, you can enable automatic rotation. For Redwood-managed configuration, we support updating the key ARN and rolling the components that depend on it. There’s a controlled rollout procedure.

[10:47] Jonas Weber: And HSM.

[10:49] Naomi Feldman: If you need “HSM-backed,” AWS KMS keys are backed by HSMs by default (FIPS 140-2 level, depending on region). If you need dedicated CloudHSM, we need to confirm integration because that can affect the key interface. Some customers treat KMS as sufficient for the requirement.

[11:11] Maya Patel: We have a policy that says HSM or KMS is acceptable as long as it’s FIPS validated. We should document which.

[11:18] Naomi Feldman: We can share our standard statement. We won’t claim a specific FIPS level for your environment without verification, but we’ll point to AWS KMS compliance and our design.

[11:30] Chris Donnelly: For on-prem, we’re not there yet, but it might happen. If we go on-prem, we have Thales HSM.

[11:38] Fatima Noor: For on-prem Private, the pattern is: you operate the cluster and provide the HSM integration point. Redwood can integrate via standard interfaces depending on the vault / KMS layer you use. We’d scope that as part of the on-prem package. Not trying to be vague — it’s just different depending on if it’s PKCS#11, HashiCorp Vault with HSM, etc.

[12:04] Chris Donnelly: Ok. Today we’re AWS.

[12:07] Fatima Noor: Great. Then it’s pretty straightforward: CMK for object storage exports, CMK for the database volume if you use a managed DB, and secrets in AWS Secrets Manager with KMS.

[12:21] Maya Patel: Do you encrypt prompt/output at rest inside the system.

[12:26] Fatima Noor: For metadata logs and system state, yes. For prompts/outputs, again, in regulated mode we recommend you do not persist them in the Redwood control plane. For Private deployments, you can configure request body logging to be disabled, and caching settings too.

[12:44] Chris Donnelly: Wait, caching — KV cache. That’s in memory. Does that count as at-rest.

[12:50] Fatima Noor: KV cache is in GPU memory / RAM, ephemeral, and it’s cleared as part of runtime lifecycle. We don’t persist KV cache to disk. For long-running services, we isolate per tenant. But if your policy treats any memory persistence as “storage,” we can talk through how it works.

[13:11] Maya Patel: It’s mostly fine, we just need to know it’s not written to disk.

[13:15] Fatima Noor: Correct.

[13:18] Jonas Weber: Another question: admin access. Who at Redwood can access our Private deployment.

[13:24] Naomi Feldman: By default, none. Access is controlled by you. If you opt into support access, it’s time-bound and logged. We do break-glass with approvals, and those actions are auditable.

[13:38] Maya Patel: Those break-glass events show in the audit logs?

[13:41] Fatima Noor: Yes, they show as “support_access_granted” and “support_session_started/ended,” with the actor set to Redwood support principal.

[13:52] Chris Donnelly: That’s important.

[13:54] Avery Johnson: We can include that in the doc we send.

[13:57] Chris Donnelly: We also need to know if the logs include data location. Like region.

[14:03] Fatima Noor: Yes, region and availability zone if applicable, for Private deployments. For multi-region setups, it’s explicit.

[14:13] Maya Patel: Residency is a question. We are US-only.

[14:16] Avery Johnson: Yep, we’ve been scoping US-only.

[14:19] Jonas Weber: Can we restrict that nothing leaves our VPC. Like the control plane.

[14:24] Fatima Noor: In Private, control plane is inside your network boundary. There are options for how we do license checks / updates. We can do an offline mode for restricted environments, but it’s a more involved setup. For most VPC Private, it’s still within your AWS account and we use VPC endpoints for the necessary services.

[14:46] Chris Donnelly: Ok.

[14:47] Maya Patel: Back to audit logs: do you have a list of event types. We need to map to our policy.

[14:54] Fatima Noor: Yes, we have an internal list and we can share the customer-facing doc. Off the top: auth.login_success/failure, api_key.created/rotated/revoked, role.assigned/removed, policy.updated, model.pinned/unpinned, deployment.scaled, inference.request, inference.error, export.config_updated, and support.access events.

[15:24] Maya Patel: Perfect.

[15:26] Chris Donnelly: We should talk Splunk detail. If it’s S3 JSON lines, what’s the file naming and frequency.

[15:33] Fatima Noor: Typical is partitioned by date/hour: s3://bucket/audit/YYYY/MM/DD/HH/*.jsonl.gz. Frequency can be every 5 minutes, 15 minutes, hourly. Compression: gzip.

[15:49] Chris Donnelly: Ok that’s fine. And is it exactly once.

[15:54] Fatima Noor: It’s at-least-once. So you need to dedupe based on event_id. That’s standard.

[16:01] Chris Donnelly: Great.

[16:03] Jonas Weber: And retention. You said you can set local retention. Does the audit store use the same key.

[16:11] Fatima Noor: It uses the same at-rest encryption mechanism as the underlying storage (EBS or managed storage). So yes, if your volumes are KMS-encrypted, that’s covered.

[16:24] Maya Patel: We also require quarterly access review. Can the audit logs tell us who has what roles.

[16:31] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs will show the changes, but for access review you usually also want a point-in-time export of current roles. The Console supports exporting current user/role mapping. That export itself is also logged.

[16:46] Maya Patel: Ok.

[16:48] Chris Donnelly: I have a question about “token-level logging.” Some vendors log the whole conversation for troubleshooting.

[16:55] Fatima Noor: We don’t do token-level content logging by default. In Console you’ll see aggregate token usage per request, not the tokens themselves. For troubleshooting, you can enable tracing hooks, but again you control what content is included.

[17:12] Chris Donnelly: Good.

[17:14] Avery Johnson: Competitors aside, we’ve seen other providers say “we’re compliant” and then it’s all hand-wavy. So we want to make sure you get specifics.

[17:23] Maya Patel: Yeah, like Bedrock gives you CloudTrail but it’s not always enough.

[17:28] Chris Donnelly: And Azure OpenAI is weird because half the logs are in Azure Monitor and it’s not consistent.

[17:35] Fatima Noor: Right. Our goal is a stable audit event stream that’s purpose-built for inference + admin actions.

[17:43] Jonas Weber: Will you sign something about retention.

[17:46] Avery Johnson: That’s more in the DPA/SLA track. But we can give you a retention statement as part of the evidence pack.

[17:54] Naomi Feldman: Just to be clear, for Private deployment in your account, you control retention. For hosted, we have defaults and contractual terms. We’ll align to your model.

[18:06] Maya Patel: Makes sense.

[18:08] Chris Donnelly: Another detail: do you log changes to model versions. Like you pinned model X and then updated.

[18:15] Fatima Noor: Yes, there are “model_version_pinned” and “rollout_policy_updated” events. Also “fallback_triggered” can be emitted if you enable that, but that’s more operational telemetry than audit.

[18:33] Chris Donnelly: We might want that too, actually. For incident reconstruction.

[18:37] Fatima Noor: Yep, we can include it.

[18:40] Maya Patel: Who has access to the logs. Is there a way to restrict the Console.

[18:47] Naomi Feldman: RBAC. You can restrict audit log viewing and exporting to a “Security Auditor” role, separate from dev roles.

[18:55] Maya Patel: Good.

[18:57] Chris Donnelly: Ok, KMS again. For the inference payload in transit, TLS. Do you support mTLS.

[19:05] Fatima Noor: For Private deployments, yes, we can do mTLS at the ingress if you’re using your own gateway / service mesh. Redwood itself supports standard TLS termination; mTLS is typically implemented via Envoy/Istio or your gateway.

[19:20] Chris Donnelly: Fine.

[19:22] Jonas Weber: Are you SOC 2.

[19:24] Naomi Feldman: Yes, SOC 2 Type II. We have a standard process to share the report under NDA. I’ll send the evidence pack index and the request steps.

[19:36] Maya Patel: Ok.

[19:38] Avery Johnson: I want to make sure we answer the main “checkbox” items for your procurement. Maya, can you list what you need written.

[19:47] Maya Patel: Written: audit log fields and event types; export to S3 and/or Splunk; KMS CMK support; key rotation guidance; support access logging.

[20:01] Avery Johnson: Great.

[20:03] Fatima Noor: One more nuance: if you do Splunk HEC direct, we need allowlisting and we’ll send over the egress IPs, or we do it inside your VPC so it’s just internal.

[20:16] Chris Donnelly: We prefer internal.

[20:18] Fatima Noor: Then S3 path is easiest.

[20:21] Chris Donnelly: For S3, do you assume cross-account.

[20:24] Fatima Noor: No, same account if Private is in your account. If Dedicated is in our account, then it would be cross-account. For you, again, we’ve been talking Private.

[20:35] Chris Donnelly: Yep.

[20:37] Maya Patel: This is good. Anything else we should ask.

[20:41] Jonas Weber: Incident response. If there’s an incident, can we get audit logs quickly.

[20:46] Naomi Feldman: Yes. For Private, you have them. For hosted/dedicated, we provide them via export and under incident process. We can walk you through our IR policy in the evidence pack.

[21:01] Avery Johnson: Do you want to talk timeline. Like when do we do the next step.

[21:06] Chris Donnelly: I want the sample payload first so I can test Splunk parsing.

[21:10] Fatima Noor: Done.

[21:12] Maya Patel: And I’ll need your SOC 2 access instructions. Not the whole report today, but the process.

[21:18] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[21:20] Avery Johnson: Cool. Let’s do a quick recap and we’ll end early if that’s ok.

[21:25] Fatima Noor: Recap: audit logs include actor, action, resource, request_id, model/version, tokens, latency, IP, region, status. Exports: S3 JSONL gzip partitioned by time; at-least-once delivery, dedupe by event_id. Retention is configurable in Private and you can keep minimal local buffering.

[21:48] Naomi Feldman: And KMS: customer-managed CMK in your AWS account for at-rest encryption and S3 export encryption; key rotation supported; support access is opt-in and audited.

[22:02] Maya Patel: Great.

[22:03] Chris Donnelly: Works for me.

[22:05] Avery Johnson: Awesome. We’ll send the follow-ups by Thursday. And I’ll schedule a 30-min follow-up for next week to walk through the questionnaire sections.

[22:14] Maya Patel: Thanks.

[22:15] Chris Donnelly: Thanks.

[22:16] Jonas Weber: Thank you.

[22:18] (Call continues with light scheduling / goodbyes; transcription ends)

Notes: Fireflies auto-transcript appears to have ended early; remaining time was scheduling / off-topic.
